faq.a: Because the patch of skin over the lateral deltoid is small and triangular, resembling a military badge.
faq.q: Why is the sensory loss described as a ‘regimental badge’ area?

faq.a: Mild stretch injuries often improve with physiotherapy; complete transection usually needs surgical repair.
faq.q: Can the axillary nerve recover without surgery?

faq.a: Suprascapular loss affects supraspinatus (initial abduction) and infraspinatus (external rotation), while axillary loss spares the first 15° of abduction and does not affect infraspinatus.
faq.q: What differentiates axillary nerve injury from suprascapular nerve injury?

exam: A patient presents after a fall with an anterior shoulder dislocation. What is the next immediate step and why? — Perform a gentle closed reduction promptly to relieve neurovascular compromise, then reassess axillary nerve function.

During examination you note loss of shoulder abduction beyond 15°. Which nerve is most likely injured and what structure protects it? — Axillary nerve; it runs through the quadrangular space bounded by teres minor, teres major, long head of triceps and surgical neck of humerus.

How would you differentiate an axillary nerve lesion from a C5 radiculopathy? — Axillary lesion causes isolated deltoid weakness and lateral shoulder sensory loss; C5 radiculopathy adds biceps weakness and sensory loss over the lateral forearm.

In a low‑resource clinic you cannot obtain an MRI. How do you confirm an axillary nerve injury? — Rely on focused history, physical exam (deltoid strength, regimental badge sensation) and plain shoulder X‑ray to rule out fracture/dislocation.

A patient with sickle cell disease presents with sudden shoulder pain and weakness. What tropical‑related cause should you consider? — Vaso‑occlusive infarction of the humeral head causing secondary axillary nerve compression; manage pain and consider transfusion.

Why is a high‑velocity shoulder injury more likely to damage the axillary nerve than a low‑energy strain? — The nerve lies close to the surgical neck; fracture or dislocation from high‑energy trauma directly stretches or transects it.

What physiotherapy regimen is appropriate after an isolated axillary nerve stretch injury? — Early passive range‑of‑motion, progressing to active deltoid strengthening once pain subsides, avoiding overhead loading for 6 weeks.

When would you refer a patient with suspected axillary nerve injury for surgical exploration? — Persistent motor deficit after 3‑4 months, evidence of nerve transection on imaging, or worsening functional loss.
ai.title: Axillary Nerve
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor muscles and skin over the lateral shoulder. Injury causes deltoid weakness, loss of shoulder abduction and a characteristic sensory patch. Understanding its course helps diagnose shoulder trauma in low‑resource settings.

b: Motor: deltoid (abduction 15‑90°) and teres minor (external rotation)
Sensory: skin over the ‘regimental badge’ area (lateral deltoid region)
Typical injury pattern: shoulder dislocation, humeral fracture, or compression
sections.p: The axillary nerve is a terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus, carrying fibers from C5 and C6. It exits the axilla through the quadrangular space to innervate the deltoid and teres minor and provides cutaneous sensation over the lateral shoulder.

b: Length ~6 cm from origin to deltoid insertion
Contains both motor and sensory fibers
sections.p: The nerve arises from the posterior cord, runs posterior to the humeral neck, and passes through the quadrangular space bounded by teres minor, teres major, long head of triceps, and surgical neck of humerus.

b: Posterior circumflex humeral artery – accompanies nerve
Teres minor – forms superior border of quadrangular space
sections.p: In the quadrangular space it lies deep to the posterior circumflex humeral artery and superficial to the surgical neck of the humerus. It is vulnerable during anterior shoulder dislocation and humeral neck fractures.

b: Posterior circumflex humeral artery – main source
sections.p: The axillary nerve receives its vascular supply from branches of the posterior circumflex humeral artery, which itself arises from the axillary artery.
Motor fibers to deltoid (especially middle fibers) and teres minor; sensory fibers to the skin over the lateral shoulder (regimental badge area).
Enables shoulder abduction from 15° to 90° via deltoid contraction and external rotation via teres minor. Sensory input informs the brain of pressure and pain over the lateral shoulder.

b: Loss of sensation over regimental badge area
sections.p: Axillary nerve injury is common after anterior shoulder dislocation, humeral neck fractures, or compression from poorly placed crutches. In low‑resource settings, delayed presentation and lack of imaging increase morbidity.

t.b: Confirms motor and sensory loss; if positive, indicates axillary nerve injury – guides further imaging or referral
Detects dislocation or humeral neck fracture; if unavailable, rely on history and exam to decide urgent reduction
Assesses soft‑tissue injury and nerve continuity; if not, monitor recovery clinically

b: Ask patient to abduct arm against resistance – weakness suggests axillary nerve lesion
Test sensation over lateral shoulder with light touch or pinprick
Observe for shoulder droop when arm is relaxed
sections.p: Focus on the deltoid’s ability to abduct the arm and the sensory patch. Remember the quadrangular space boundaries to explain why fractures of the surgical neck threaten the nerve.

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive weakness of the arm leading to inability to lift the hand
Severe shoulder pain with deformity suggesting dislocation or fracture
Rapidly spreading sensory loss indicating possible brachial plexus involvement
